title: Building a life
hookLine: the householder stage: a hero wins his war and wants the forest, and his family talks him into staying
tomorrow: the Buddha's son came asking for his inheritance. what did he get?

lines: SELL THE STUFF, MOVE TO A CABIN.
cards: Some people dream of quitting everything: sell the stuff, move to a cabin, finally get spiritual. The Mahabharata has a hero who tried. Here's the odd part.
Yudhishthira has just won the great war, and the kingdom with it. Grieving all the dead, he says: I don't want it. I'll go to the forest, live on roots, and leave the world behind.
An epic full of forest sages might be expected to cheer him on. Instead his brothers and his wife Draupadi talk him out of it, one after another.

teach.b: Why? Read the Shanti Parva, the book of peace, and the arguments pile up. His brother Nakula praises the household as the life the others depend on.
Draupadi tells him a king who walks away leaves his people unprotected. The sage Vyasa joins in. In the end, Yudhishthira takes the throne.
That's the puzzle solved, and it's a real Hindu teaching.
The second of the four stages is grihastha, the householder: work, marriage, children, money, duty. Far from second best, the Laws of Manu call it the support of all the others.

teach.h: EVERY STAGE LIVES BY THIS ONE.
teach.b: As every creature lives by the air, every other stage lives by the householder, who feeds the student, the forest-dweller and the wandering ascetic. In this picture, a busy parent isn't behind the monk.
The parent is holding the monk up.

So Manu gives the householder five daily offerings: to the sages, by study; to the ancestors; to the gods; to all creatures, with a little food set out; and to people, by welcoming guests. Notice what the list does.
It turns an ordinary day into a ring of gifts: the mind fed, the dead remembered, the gods honored, the animals fed, the stranger welcomed.
The spiritual life of this stage isn't somewhere else. It's in the kitchen, the job, the bills, the open door. Yudhishthira's forest could wait.
It had its own season, later.

how: Hindu tradition honors the householder stage, grihastha, as the one that supports all the others. The Laws of Manu give the householder five daily offerings: study, offerings to the ancestors and the gods, food set out for creatures, and welcoming guests.

o: a plan to buy a house and pay off the mortgage early
the householder stage: work, family and duty as practice
the years spent saving up for a long retreat

games.q: the householder puzzle: tap the pairs.
p: won the war, wanted the forest
a king who leaves, leaves people unprotected

s: in Hindu tradition, the householder stage is a lesser, worldly time
the Laws of Manu call it the support of all the other stages.
after the war, Yudhishthira wanted to leave the kingdom for the forest
in the Shanti Parva, his family and the sage Vyasa argue him back to the throne.
Manu's five daily offerings include welcoming guests
hospitality to guests is the householder's offering to people.

games.q: a coworker says she'll "get spiritual" once the kids are grown and the house is paid off. what does the householder teaching suggest?
o: the household years are a stage of practice too: study, family, food for others, guests.
she's right: real spiritual practice is for after your duties are done.
she should quit now; duty and spirit can't share one house.
games.why: Manu calls the householder the support of every other stage, with five daily offerings: study, ancestors, gods, creatures and guests.

practice: Count on your fingers the things that depend on you this week: a job, a person, a pet, a plant, a bill. For each one, a quiet thank-you that you get to carry it, even the heavy ones.
Then rest your hands and breathe for the rest of the time.

wordCard.voice: Building a life: grihastha, the householder stage. Work, family and duty, held up as a practice of their own.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the householder; the second of the four stages of life.

carryVoice: Your line: the householder. Manu says every other stage lives by this one, and the kitchen counts. That's day 1682.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, early sections (Yudhishthira's grief and wish to renounce the kingdom for the forest; the arguments of Arjuna, Bhima, Nakula, Draupadi and Vyasa; he accepts the throne)
Laws of Manu 3.77-78 (as all creatures live by air, the other orders live by the householder; therefore the householder's order is the most excellent)
Laws of Manu 3.70 (the five great sacrifices: study, offerings to the ancestors, the burnt offering to the gods, the bali offering to beings, hospitality to guests)
